patient_selection.evidence: Patients with known, treated, or suspected brain tumors underwent compressed sensing-sensitivity encoding accelerated 3D T1-echo-spoiled gradient echo or 3D T2-FLAIR sequences in addition to the corresponding conventional acquisition as part of their clinical brain MR imaging.
patient_selection.rationale: Abstract-only record states the clinical population but gives no enrolment rule (consecutive, random or convenience) and no inclusion/exclusion criteria.

index_test.evidence: Two neuroradiologists blinded to sequence and patient information independently evaluated both the accelerated and corresponding conventional acquisitions.
index_test.rationale: Readers were explicitly blinded to which sequence was accelerated and read the two acquisitions independently.

reference_standard.evidence: The sequences were evaluated on 4- or 5-point Likert scales for overall image quality, SNR, extent/severity of artifacts, and gray-white junction and lesion boundary sharpness.
reference_standard.rationale: The conventional clinical acquisition served as the reference and was scored on pre-specified Likert scales by the same readers who were blinded to sequence type.

flow_timing.evidence: in addition to the corresponding conventional acquisition as part of their clinical brain MR imaging
flow_timing.rationale: Accelerated and conventional acquisitions were obtained in the same clinical examination, so the interval is effectively zero and every patient contributed a paired comparison.

app_patient_selection.evidence: Patients with known, treated, or suspected brain tumors underwent compressed sensing-sensitivity encoding accelerated 3D T1-echo-spoiled gradient echo or 3D T2-FLAIR sequences
app_patient_selection.rationale: Real clinical brain MRI patients with pathology, matching the population of interest for whether acceleration preserves diagnostic content.

app_index_test.evidence: Compressed sensing-sensitivity encoding accelerated 3D T1-echo-spoiled gradient echo and T2-FLAIR sequences of the brain show image quality similar to that of standard acquisitions with reduced scan time.
app_index_test.rationale: The index test is a prospectively acquired accelerated reconstruction of routine brain sequences, directly matching the review question.

app_reference_standard.evidence: This study compares the image quality of compressed sensing-sensitivity encoding accelerated imaging with conventional MR imaging sequences.
app_reference_standard.rationale: The conventional standard-of-care acquisition plus expert neuroradiologist reading is the intended reference standard for this review.

patient_selection.evidence: we selected 46 scans from consecutive patients undergoing clinically indicated MRI brain examinations from the image archive of the department
patient_selection.rationale: Consecutive sampling from clinically indicated examinations is explicitly stated, and no case-control enrichment or restrictive exclusion is described.

index_test.evidence: The images were shown to 2 board-certified neuroradiologists in random order and did not contain any information regarding origin (ie, before/after correction).
index_test.rationale: Readers were blinded to whether an image was corrected by the network and images were presented in random order, using a pre-specified 0-4 scale.

reference_standard.evidence: Because artifact-free reference images were not available for these 28 clinical motion cases, all artifact-corrupted input and artifact-corrected output images (962 in total) were rated on a section-by-section level in a blinded reader study
reference_standard.rationale: No artifact-free or fully sampled reference existed for the real-patient evaluation cohort; the only ground truth was simulation-derived and applied to two volumes.

flow_timing.evidence: All volumes that were deemed artifact-free by the radiologist (18 of 46) were then used to generate the synthetic training and test dataset (16 and 2 volumes, respectively).
flow_timing.rationale: Flow of all 46 scans into training and test subsets is fully accounted for, and the before/after comparison uses the same images, so the interval is zero.

app_patient_selection.evidence: Common indications included known or suspected intracranial tumor (primary or metastatic, including follow-up), known or suspected acute ischemic stroke (including follow-up), known or suspected demyelinating disease, dementia
app_patient_selection.rationale: Routine clinical brain MRI patients with a broad spectrum of neurological indications, matching the review population.

app_index_test.evidence: The presented network-based motion artifact correction represents a purely retrospective correction technique, requiring only standard-magnitude images from a traditional DICOM repository
app_index_test.rationale: The index test is deep-learning motion-artifact correction applied to magnitude DICOMs, not an accelerated reconstruction from undersampled k-space, and explicitly saves no scan time.

app_reference_standard.evidence: all artifact-corrupted input and artifact-corrected output images (962 in total) were rated on a section-by-section level in a blinded reader study using the 0–4 qualitative scale described previously
app_reference_standard.rationale: The comparator was the uncorrected image rated for artifact severity rather than a fully sampled acquisition or diagnostic ground truth, so preservation of diagnostic content is not directly assessed.

patient_selection.evidence: STUDY TYPE: Prospective healthy volunteer study. SUBJECTS: Eight healthy subjects.
patient_selection.rationale: A convenience sample of eight healthy volunteers with no stated recruitment rule excludes the patients and pathology the diagnostic question concerns.

index_test.evidence: Independent radiological diagnostic quality assessments of accelerated 3D MR brain datasets were carried out by four experienced neuro-radiologists who were blinded to the acceleration factor and to the subject.
index_test.rationale: Readers were blinded to acceleration factor and subject identity and graded independently using a previously reported scoring key.

reference_standard.evidence: Despite having lower scores than fully sampled datasets, the majority of the compressed sensing (CS) accelerated brain datasets with k-space sampling order optimization
reference_standard.rationale: Fully sampled datasets served as the reference and were graded by the same radiologists who were blinded to acceleration factor.

flow_timing.evidence: (19/24 datasets by Radiologist 1, 24/24 datasets by Radiologist 2 and 16/24 datasets by Radiologist 3) were graded to be fully diagnostic
flow_timing.rationale: Four readers are stated but results are reported for only three, and the abstract does not describe whether all acquired datasets entered the analysis.

app_patient_selection.evidence: STUDY TYPE: Prospective healthy volunteer study. SUBJECTS: Eight healthy subjects.
app_patient_selection.rationale: Healthy volunteers contain no pathology, so the study cannot speak to whether accelerated reconstruction preserves lesion-level diagnostic content in patients.

app_index_test.evidence: Optimization of the k-space sampling order was important for preserving contrast in accelerated scans.
app_index_test.rationale: Compressed-sensing accelerated 3D brain acquisition is precisely the class of index test the review addresses.

app_reference_standard.evidence: Despite having lower scores than fully sampled datasets, the majority of the compressed sensing (CS) accelerated brain datasets with k-space sampling order optimization
app_reference_standard.rationale: Fully sampled acquisition graded by expert neuroradiologists is the reference standard the review question assumes.

patient_selection.evidence: Forty subjects underwent brain MR imaging examinations on 6 scanners from 5 institutions. Standard of care and accelerated datasets were acquired for each subject
patient_selection.rationale: Prospective and multicentre, but the abstract gives no sampling frame, no consecutive or random enrolment statement and no eligibility criteria.

index_test.evidence: Randomized, side-by-side, multiplanar datasets (360 series) were presented blinded to 2 neuroradiologists and rated for apparent SNR, image sharpness, artifacts, anatomic/lesion conspicuity, image contrast, and gray-white differentiation
index_test.rationale: Image-quality readers were blinded to reconstruction type, datasets were randomised, and the rating features were pre-specified.

reference_standard.evidence: Standard of care, accelerated scans, and accelerated-deep learning were subjected to NeuroQuant quantitative analysis and classified by a neuroradiologist into clinical disease categories.
reference_standard.rationale: Standard of care is an appropriate reference, but the abstract does not state whether the neuroradiologist assigning clinical disease categories was blinded to reconstruction type.

flow_timing.evidence: Standard of care and accelerated datasets were acquired for each subject, and the accelerated scans were enhanced with deep learning processing.
flow_timing.rationale: Every subject received both the accelerated and the standard-of-care acquisition in the same session, giving a zero interval and the same reference for all.

app_patient_selection.evidence: Forty subjects underwent brain MR imaging examinations on 6 scanners from 5 institutions.
app_patient_selection.rationale: Multicentre, multi-scanner clinical brain MRI subjects assigned to clinical disease categories, matching the intended review population.

app_index_test.evidence: 60% accelerated volumetric MR imaging sequences processed with a commercially available, vendor-agnostic, DICOM-based, deep learning tool (SubtleMR) compared with that of standard of care
app_index_test.rationale: A prospectively acquired 60% accelerated sequence with deep-learning enhancement is directly the index test class of interest.

app_reference_standard.evidence: There was no difference in quantitative volumetric biomarkers or clinical classification for standard of care and accelerated-deep learning datasets.
app_reference_standard.rationale: Standard-of-care acquisition with expert reading and quantitative volumetrics is the reference standard the review question assumes.

patient_selection.evidence: The selection process favored cases with more subtle pathologies for the 4X track and more obvious pathologies for the 8X track
patient_selection.rationale: Only 18 volumes reached reader evaluation and they were purposively hand-picked by a neuroradiologist to be enriched for particular pathology conspicuity, not consecutive or random.

index_test.evidence: basing their overall ranking on the quality of the depiction of the pathology using the ground truth as a reference
index_test.rationale: Radiologists were blinded to team identity but interpreted the reconstructions with the fully sampled reference image visible, so index-test reading was not independent of the reference standard.

reference_standard.evidence: For the ground truth images, we followed the previous convention [27] to use root sum-of-squares images.
reference_standard.rationale: The reference is the fully sampled acquisition reconstructed by root sum-of-squares, an accepted ground truth despite the acknowledged phase and background-noise drawbacks.

flow_timing.evidence: We applied retrospective downsampling to fully-sampled MRIs and provided the downsampled data to challenge participants.
flow_timing.rationale: Undersampling was applied retrospectively to the same raw k-space so the interval is zero, and all radiologists rated all selected cases.

app_patient_selection.evidence: Selected cases included both intraaxial and extraaxial tumors, strokes, microvascular ischemia, white matter lesions, edema, surgical cavities, as well as postsurgical changes and hardware including craniotomies and ventricular shunts.
app_patient_selection.rationale: Clinical brain scans spanning a broad, clinically representative range of neuroimaging pathology.

app_index_test.evidence: As a result, challenge models are likely to require further fine-tuning training before application to clinical data.
app_index_test.rationale: Reconstructions came from research challenge entries using pseudo-equispaced retrospective masks that the authors state do not match clinical sampling, so they differ from deployed accelerated reconstruction.

app_reference_standard.evidence: we quantitatively evaluated it using the fully-sampled data as gold standards
app_reference_standard.rationale: The fully sampled acquisition combined with expert radiologist reading is exactly the reference standard the review question specifies.

patient_selection.evidence: In this study, 172 patients undergoing 1.5 T brain MRI were scanned with a more commonly used susceptibility sequence
patient_selection.rationale: Only the abstract is available; it reports the cohort size and setting but no consecutive or random enrolment rule and no eligibility criteria.

index_test.evidence: Two radiologists blinded to the acquisition technique scored each sequence for visualization of pathology, motion and signal dropout artifacts, image noise, visualization of normal anatomy
index_test.rationale: Readers were explicitly blinded to acquisition technique and scored a pre-specified set of image-quality and pathology-visualisation features.

reference_standard.evidence: Superiority testing was performed to compare Wave-SWI to T2*w-GRE, and non-inferiority testing with 15% margin was performed to compare Wave-SWI to standard SWI.
reference_standard.rationale: Conventional 3D SWI and 2D T2*w-GRE are accepted standard-of-care comparators, read by the same blinded radiologists against a pre-specified non-inferiority margin.

flow_timing.evidence: In this study, 172 patients undergoing 1.5 T brain MRI were scanned with a more commonly used susceptibility sequence (standard SWI or T2*w-GRE) and a highly accelerated Wave-SWI sequence.
flow_timing.rationale: Patients did not all receive the same reference sequence (standard SWI for some, T2*w-GRE for others), and the abstract does not report how patients were allocated or whether all 172 were analysed.

app_patient_selection.evidence: compare highly accelerated Wave-CAIPI SWI (Wave-SWI) with two alternative standard sequences, conventional three-dimensional SWI and two-dimensional T2*-weighted Gradient-Echo (T2*w-GRE), in patients undergoing routine brain MRI at 1.5 T
app_patient_selection.rationale: A large cohort of patients undergoing routine clinical brain MRI, matching the review population.

app_index_test.evidence: Wave-CAIPI (Controlled Aliasing in Parallel Imaging) enables dramatic reduction in acquisition time of 3D MRI sequences such as 3D susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) but has not been clinically evaluated at 1.5 T
app_index_test.rationale: Prospectively acquired, highly accelerated Wave-CAIPI reconstruction of a routine brain sequence is directly the index test class of interest.

app_reference_standard.evidence: Wave-SWI was non-inferior to standard SWI for visualization of normal anatomy and pathology, signal dropout artifacts, and overall image quality (all p < 0.001).
app_reference_standard.rationale: Conventional standard-of-care susceptibility sequences read by expert radiologists for pathology visualisation match the reference standard the review question assumes.
